essays.title: Freeriding Isn't a Discipline. It's a Philosophy.
essays.subtitle: Freeride skiing is headed toward the Olympics and the culture that built it has reason to be nervous.

body.text: Freeride skiing isn't just another Olympic discipline. It's a culture. Here's why Olympic inclusion risks costing freeriding the soul that made it matter.
Every sport has competition. Not every culture should become an Olympic event.
Freeride skiing may be headed to the Olympics. But freeriding was never a discipline. It's a culture built to escape the very rules the Games would impose.

I understand why people are excited about freeride skiing joining the Olympics. Inclusion means more funding, more visibility, and more opportunity for athletes; and they deserve every bit of it. But I can't shake the feeling that making freeride an Olympic sport risks defeating the very reason freeriding exists.

Freeriding was never born from a desire to win medals. It was born from a desire to escape boundaries. It never asked, "How do I score the most points?" It asked, "What's the best line on this mountain?" Those aren't the same question; and the difference between them is the whole argument.
Freeride Was Born as a Rebellion
Freeriding didn't evolve out of Olympic skiing. It evolved as a reaction against it.

The early pioneers came from racing, moguls, and traditional competition; but many walked away because skiing had become too confined by gates, courses, judges, and predetermined definitions of what "good skiing" was supposed to look like. Big-mountain skiing asked a completely different question: what happens when there are no gates? Instead of skiing the course someone else built, you built your own. That philosophical shift is arguably the birth of freeriding itself.
Freeride Was Never Meant to Fit Inside a Rulebook

For decades, freeride skiing existed almost as the opposite of Olympic sport. It wasn't born on groomed race courses or in national training academies. It grew out of a generation of skiers: Shane McConkey, Rob and Scott Gaffney, Kent Kreitler, Seth Morrison, Mike Douglas, Jonny Mosely, Jeremy Nobis, Ingrid Backstrom, CR Johnson, and countless others who simply looked at mountains differently. Many had backgrounds in racing or traditional competition, but they weren't trying to perfect the systems that already existed. They were trying to escape them.

They weren't chasing stopwatches. They weren't chasing medals. They were chasing possibility. The philosophy was simple: the mountain wasn't a course someone else designed; it was a blank canvas waiting to be interpreted.

That philosophy is written directly into one of the earliest IFSA newsletters, where Shane McConkey described competitive freeskiing as a discipline judged on line choice, fluidity, style, control, aggressiveness, and creativity; not simply tricks, speed, or technical execution. The goal was never standardization. It was expression.
The Original IFSA Was Built Around the Athlete, Not the Institution

When Shane McConkey and Lhotse Merriam Hawk founded the IFSA in 1996, the vision wasn't to create another governing body. It was to build an athlete-first organization where, in the group's own words, "the freerider remains our bottom line." That's a very different philosophy from building a system around national federations and Olympic qualification. The organization existed to protect freeriding, not redefine it.
Freeriding Was Built by a Culture, Not an Institution

One of the things that makes freeriding unique is that it wasn't built from the top down. Not by Olympic committees. Not by governing bodies. It was built by skiers, photographers, filmmakers, and ski companies willing to take risks, by independent events, mountain towns, and local communities. The IFSA. The Freeride World Tour. Warren Miller, TGR, Matchstick Productions, Poor Boyz, Level 1, Sherpas Cinema, Powder Magazine.

Unlike almost every Olympic discipline, freeriding's biggest moments often weren't competitions at all. They were movie segments. Groundbreaking first descents. A line no one thought was possible. A powder day shared with friends. People didn't grow up idolizing scorecards; they grew up watching films. The heroes of freeriding didn't become legends by accumulating medals. They became legends because they changed the way people imagined skiing itself.
Innovation Came Before Results

Shane McConkey is the perfect example. People remember him less for contest wins than for changing how skiing itself was imagined: reverse camber, reverse sidecut, fat powder skis, ski BASE, and a relentless, ridiculous creativity. His influence came from questioning assumptions; not mastering existing rules. Freeriding has always rewarded the people willing to ask "why are we doing it this way?" rather than "how do I perfect the current system?"
Olympic Sports Become Standardized

The Olympics require something every governing body wants: consistency. That means qualification systems, national governing bodies, coaching pipelines, age-group development, athlete quotas, equipment regulations, judging protocols, appeals, eligibility rules, anti-doping structures, broadcast schedules, and media obligations.

None of those things are inherently bad; many of them protect athletes and make sport more accessible. But they inevitably change what gets rewarded. As previously mentioned, Instead of asking "What's the most beautiful line on this face?" the sport gradually begins asking "What scores the highest?" That distinction changes everything.
Style Slowly Gives Way to Optimization

Every judged Olympic sport eventually trends toward optimization. Figure skating changed. Halfpipe changed. Slopestyle changed. Snowboarding changed. The athletes become better than ever, but styles become increasingly similar, because everyone is maximizing the same scoring system. Freeriding has largely resisted that trend because every mountain is different. Every rider sees a different line. Every descent tells a different story. The concern is that Olympic pressure slowly narrows that creativity. That instead of skiing the line that inspires you, athletes begin skiing the line that statistically scores best. The skiing may become more technical. But it also risks becoming less personal.
Counterculture Doesn't Always Survive Institutions

One of Mike Douglas' comments captures what many of freeriding's pioneers have felt: "When we started doing this stuff the Olympics were never a goal. We were running away from them." That sentence says everything. Freeriding didn't emerge because skiers wanted another governing body. It emerged because they wanted fewer rules, not better ones. It rejected the idea that skiing had to fit inside gates, courses, uniforms, national federations, and rigid competition formats. Bringing freeride under FIS, and eventually the Olympic movement, risks absorbing that counterculture into the exact institutions it originally formed outside of.
Natural Selection Shows What Freeriding Was Always Meant to Be

Ironically, one of the strongest arguments against Olympic freeride already exists: Natural Selection. Created by pro snowboarder Travis Rice, Natural Selection wasn't designed around television windows or rigid competition formats. It was designed around mountains. Venues are researched for years. Natural terrain is celebrated instead of replaced, features are built to fit the mountain, not the other way around. Conditions determine when the event happens, not broadcast schedules. Sometimes events aren't even streamed live, because the priority isn't television, it's capturing incredible riding and documenting it afterward, almost like filming a ski movie.

Qualification simply selects the riders. Once the event begins, the emphasis shifts away from chasing points and back toward style, creativity, snow, terrain, and vision. Natural Selection doesn't ask riders to adapt themselves to the event. It adapts the event to the mountain. That philosophy feels far closer to the roots of freeriding than traditional sport, and it's a big part of why so many people have come to prefer it over more rigidly structured tours.
The Mountain Is the Teacher

Freeriding has never simply been about skiing. It's about learning to read terrain, understanding snow, studying weather, respecting avalanche conditions, and building relationships with landscapes that change every single day. In racing, everyone skis the same course. In slopestyle, everyone hits the same features. In freeriding, everyone stands at the same start gate and then tells a completely different story.

The mountain isn't just where the event happens; the mountain teaches you how to ski. Olympic competition naturally focuses attention on competition weekends. Freeriding has historically focused attention on entire winters. That's a subtle but profound difference.
Commercialization Changes Culture

Olympic inclusion would bring enormous advantages: greater funding, larger sponsorships, television exposure, government support, national team resources, and more athletes making a living. Those are real benefits. But commercialization also changes incentives. Small independent events struggle. Grassroots organizers lose influence. Media becomes increasingly sponsor-driven. Athletes become representatives of brands and countries before they're simply skiers. The sport becomes more accessible, but often less rebellious.
Judging Creativity Is Inherently Difficult

Unlike racing, freeriding has never been purely objective. Judges evaluate style, flow, commitment, creativity, line choice, and mountain interpretation; qualities that are as artistic as they are athletic. The more pressure there is to standardize judging, the more pressure there is to reward consistency. Ironically, making judging "fairer" can make skiing less creative. Not everything beautiful can be quantified.
The Sport Risks Becoming Another Pipeline

Olympic sports create development systems. Kids begin training specifically for medals. Parents invest earlier. National federations decide funding. Coaches begin teaching which cliffs score the highest, which turns judges reward, which lines maximize points. Eventually a generation of athletes grows up learning how judges want mountains to be skied instead of discovering their own relationship with them. That may produce incredible competitors, but fewer innovators.
Not Everything Needs Olympic Validation

We tend to assume Olympic inclusion is the highest possible achievement for any sport. But that isn't necessarily true. Surfing, skateboarding, and climbing all built thriving global cultures long before Olympic recognition ever arrived. The Olympics may elevate visibility, but they don't define legitimacy. Some communities derive their entire identity precisely from existing outside traditional institutions, and freeriding is one of them.
Freeriding Was Always Bigger Than Competition

For most freeriders, the greatest memories don't happen on podiums. They happen skinning into the backcountry before sunrise. Finding untracked snow with friends. Earning every turn. Discovering a line nobody else saw. Filming a clip you'll remember forever. Laughing in the parking lot after the best day of your life.

Competition has always existed to celebrate that culture, not define it. The fear isn't that Olympic competition exists. The fear is that competition begins shaping the culture instead of the culture shaping the competition.
A Fair Counterpoint

None of this is meant to suggest the Olympics are inherently bad. They're not. Olympic inclusion would bring freeriding unprecedented visibility, funding, and legitimacy, along with opportunities for athletes around the world. More people could build careers, junior pathways and safety resources could improve, and the sport would reach audiences it never could otherwise. Even some athletes who were initially skeptical have acknowledged those benefits. So this isn't a simple "good versus bad" debate. It's a tradeoff.

The question isn't whether freeriding deserves Olympic recognition. It clearly does. The real question is whether freeriding can gain Olympic legitimacy without sacrificing the independent, creative spirit that made it worth recognizing in the first place.

At its core, freeriding isn't just another competitive discipline. It's a culture. A philosophy. A relationship with mountains that values exploration over optimization, expression over conformity, style over perfection, adventure over medals, community over bureaucracy, and creativity over standardization.

As Shane McConkey wrote in one of the earliest IFSA newsletters, the goal was never simply to grow freeskiing. It was to grow it without losing its soul. Three decades later, that's still the question worth asking. Because the day those values become secondary to scores is the day freeriding stops being free.

essays.title: The Romance of the Unconventional Life
essays.subtitle: On the peculiar business of trying to make a living without forgetting to make a life.

body.text: I’ve always been fascinated by people who seem to have found a way to live outside the ordinary expectations of life.

The people who spend their winters chasing snowstorms, their summers living out of vans, or their twenties traveling through countries they can barely pronounce. The artists who build their lives around creating things that may never make them much money. The fishermen, musicians, wanderers, and mountain-town locals who seem to have arrived at some quiet understanding that the things most people spend their lives pursuing aren’t necessarily the things they want.
There is something romantic about these people.

Not necessarily because their lives are easier, more exciting, or even particularly admirable by conventional standards, but because they seem to have questioned something that most of us are taught to accept.
The idea that there is a particular way a life is supposed to unfold.

We grow up surrounded by a fairly predictable sequence of expectations. Go to school, find a career, establish financial security, build a home, settle down, and eventually arrive at some imagined point where we can begin enjoying the life we’ve spent so many years preparing for.
There is nothing inherently wrong with that.
In fact, there is something deeply appealing about stability, about knowing where you’ll be next year, what your days will look like, and how you’ll support yourself.
But I’ve always been troubled by the assumption that this is the only sensible way to live.
Or, more specifically, by the idea that anything outside of it represents some kind of failure to grow up.
Because when I look at the people whose lives I find most interesting, very few of them seem to have followed a particularly predictable path.
And I wonder whether the real measure of a successful life has less to do with how closely it resembles the one we were told to pursue than with how honestly it reflects the things we actually value.
I think part of my fascination with unconventional living comes from the places I’ve spent my life. There is a particular kind of person you encounter in mountain towns.
Someone who might be extraordinarily talented at something that has very little practical value outside the world they’ve chosen to inhabit.

A skier who knows every line on a mountain but has never been especially interested in climbing a corporate ladder. A bartender who spends every free day exploring the backcountry. A photographer who has spent years documenting a community that most people will never know exists.
People who have organized their lives around the things they love, even when doing so requires sacrifices that might seem unreasonable to someone looking in from the outside.
I’ve always found that interesting.
Especially because many of these people are not particularly concerned with explaining themselves.
They don’t necessarily have some grand philosophy about rejecting society or redefining success.
They simply know what they want their lives to contain.
And they’ve made decisions accordingly.
Growing up around skiing, sailing, and the ocean, I was exposed to communities where people’s identities were often shaped as much by what they did outside of work as by their professions.
Someone might be a lawyer, a carpenter, a teacher, or a restaurant employee, but those titles rarely told you the most interesting things about them.
You learned more by asking where they skied, what they were building, what they were reading, or where they had disappeared to last summer.
There was a certain understanding that work was important, but it wasn’t necessarily the entirety of a person.
I think I’ve carried that understanding into my own life.
I’ve always been drawn toward experiences that make me feel as though I’m participating in something larger than the ordinary routines of daily existence.
Skiing has been one of the clearest expressions of that.

There is something about waking up before sunrise, driving through the mountains in the dark, and spending an entire day pursuing something as fleeting as good snow that seems almost irrational when you examine it too closely.
You spend money on equipment, gas, lift tickets, and countless other things simply to slide down a mountain and do it again.
Sometimes the weather is miserable. Sometimes the snow is terrible. Sometimes you spend more time waiting, hiking, or driving than actually skiing.
And yet, on the right day, none of that seems to matter.

There are moments when the snow is good, the light is right, and the people you’re with are exactly the people you want to be with, when the entire experience feels so complete that it becomes difficult to imagine what else you could possibly need.
Those moments don’t produce anything tangible.
They don’t improve your résumé or move you closer to some conventional measure of success.
They simply exist.

And I’ve always found it strange that we live in a culture so preoccupied with productivity when some of the most meaningful experiences of our lives are valuable precisely because they accomplish nothing.
Of course, the freedom to pursue those experiences is rarely as simple as it appears.
The mountain-town lifestyle is easy to romanticize from a distance.

We see the photographs of powder days, the old trucks parked beneath enormous mountains, the summer evenings spent around campfires, and the people who seem to have escaped the ordinary pressures of modern life.
What we don’t always see are the second jobs, the unreliable cars, the overdue bills, the shared houses, and the uncertainty about what happens when the season ends.
We don’t see the people who are exhausted from working late nights so they can afford to ski the following morning.
Or the quiet anxiety of realizing that the lifestyle you’ve built around freedom still requires money, healthcare, housing, and some degree of stability.
I’ve come to understand that an unconventional life isn’t necessarily a life without responsibility.
Sometimes it requires an extraordinary amount of it.
The difference is that the responsibilities are organized around a different set of priorities.
And I think that’s where the romance becomes more complicated.
It’s easy to admire someone who seems to have escaped the conventional world.
It’s harder to acknowledge the compromises that made that escape possible.
Because every choice, no matter how liberating it initially feels, closes the door on something else.
Choosing to spend your twenties traveling might mean postponing financial security.
Choosing a creative career might mean accepting years of uncertainty.
Choosing to live in a mountain town might mean fewer professional opportunities, higher living costs, or a life that becomes increasingly difficult to sustain.
And choosing stability can mean sacrificing the freedom to pursue experiences that may never come around again.
There is no arrangement in which we get to have everything.
I think that’s one of the more uncomfortable truths about adulthood.
Not that we eventually have to abandon the things we love, but that we have to decide how much we’re willing to sacrifice for them.
And perhaps that’s why the idea of an unconventional life has always appealed to me.
It represents the possibility of making those decisions consciously rather than simply accepting the priorities that have been handed to us.
But I also think there’s a danger in romanticizing freedom itself.
We tend to imagine freedom as the absence of obligations.
No fixed schedule. No one telling us where to be. No commitments preventing us from leaving whenever we want.
There is certainly something appealing about that kind of independence.
But I’ve started to wonder whether a life without obligations is necessarily a free one.
Because without some sense of purpose, direction, or responsibility, freedom can begin to feel strangely empty.
I’ve experienced moments when having an open schedule felt wonderful, and others when it made me feel completely untethered.
There is a difference between having the freedom to do anything and knowing what you actually want to do.
And I think the second is much more difficult.
When no one is telling you what your life should look like, you’re left with the uncomfortable responsibility of figuring it out for yourself.
You can no longer rely on the next expected milestone to provide a sense of progress.
There isn’t always a clear measure of whether you’re moving in the right direction.
And sometimes, the very freedom you wanted becomes the thing that makes you question yourself.
Am I making the most of my life?
Am I wasting time?
Am I pursuing something meaningful, or simply avoiding something difficult?
I think those questions are particularly familiar to people who are drawn toward creative or unconventional careers.
There is a strange contradiction in wanting to build a life around something you love while also knowing that turning it into work can change your relationship with it.
Photography is a good example.
I love photography because it gives me a reason to pay attention.
It encourages me to notice the small details of places, people, and experiences that might otherwise pass unnoticed.
The way light falls across a mountain at the end of the day. The atmosphere of a small town. The expressions on people’s faces when they’re doing something they genuinely love.
I like the idea that an image can preserve something about a moment that would otherwise disappear.
But when photography becomes a profession, it also becomes subject to deadlines, clients, budgets, expectations, and the pressure to produce work that other people find valuable.
Something that once felt entirely free becomes connected to the same structures I was hoping to avoid.
And I don’t necessarily think that’s a bad thing.
It’s simply the reality of trying to build a life around your interests.
The things we love do not exist outside the practical world.
They exist within it.
And perhaps the challenge is not to escape that reality, but to find a way to participate in it without losing sight of why those things mattered to us in the first place.
I’ve thought about this a lot in relation to the ski industry.
There is something wonderfully absurd about an entire culture built around a recreational activity.

People dedicate their lives to designing skis, filming athletes, forecasting storms, maintaining mountains, and documenting experiences that, from a purely practical perspective, aren’t necessary at all.
And yet, those experiences have created communities, friendships, careers, artistic movements, and entire ways of life.
Ski films are particularly interesting to me because they reveal how something that begins as an individual physical experience can become a form of storytelling.
The skiing itself might last only a few seconds.
A turn, a jump, a line down a mountain.
But through film, music, and the people involved, that moment becomes part of something larger.
A representation of a particular place, time, community, or way of seeing the world.
I think that’s why I’ve always been drawn toward the idea of making ski films.
Not simply because I love skiing, but because I love the culture that exists around it.
The personalities, the histories, the humor, the strange traditions, and the people who have spent their lives pursuing something that doesn’t always make sense to the rest of the world.
There is a kind of sincerity in that commitment that I find difficult not to admire.
But I also know that building a career in a creative industry is not the same as living inside a ski film.
There are ordinary days, difficult clients, financial pressures, repetitive tasks, and compromises that never appear in the finished product.
And I think learning to accept those realities without becoming cynical is part of growing up.
Perhaps maturity isn’t abandoning the romantic ideas we had about life.
Perhaps it’s learning how to sustain them when they become complicated.
I sometimes think about the people who have spent decades living in mountain towns.
Not the people who arrived for a season and left with a collection of photographs, but the ones who stayed.
The people who raised families, opened businesses, endured difficult winters, watched their communities change, and continued building their lives around the places they loved.
I find those people more interesting than the romantic image of someone who is perpetually traveling.
Because staying somewhere requires a different kind of commitment.
It’s easy to fall in love with a place when you’re only experiencing its most beautiful moments.
It’s another thing entirely to remain there through the ordinary ones.
To experience the bad weather, the economic uncertainty, the changing community, and the inevitable realization that no place can permanently provide the feeling you had when you first discovered it.
I think there’s something deeply meaningful about choosing to belong somewhere, even after the novelty has disappeared.
And perhaps that’s another contradiction I’ve been trying to understand.
I’ve always wanted the freedom to go wherever I want.
But I’ve also wanted places that feel like home.
I’ve wanted adventure, spontaneity, and the ability to change direction whenever something interesting appears.
But I’ve also wanted meaningful relationships, familiar routines, and a sense that I’m building something that will last.
For a long time, I thought those desires were somehow incompatible.
That choosing stability meant giving up freedom, and choosing freedom meant accepting a life without roots.
But I’m beginning to think that the most interesting lives are often built somewhere between those extremes.
Not through the complete rejection of convention, but through the willingness to decide which conventions are actually worth keeping.
There is nothing inherently meaningful about being unconventional.
A person can reject every traditional expectation and still end up living a life that feels empty or directionless.
And someone else can follow a relatively ordinary path while creating a life filled with curiosity, love, adventure, and genuine satisfaction.
I think the difference lies in whether those choices are made deliberately.
Whether we understand what we’re pursuing and why.
And whether we’re willing to accept the consequences of the lives we choose.
I’ve also started to question the way we talk about success.
We tend to measure it through things that can be easily compared.
Income, job titles, property, recognition, professional accomplishments.
These measures are convenient because they create the appearance of objectivity.
We can look at two people and decide, based on a handful of visible facts, which one seems to be doing better.
But I think that kind of comparison overlooks almost everything that makes a life meaningful to the person living it.
How much time do they spend with people they love?
Do they enjoy the ordinary hours of their days?
Are they curious about the world?
Do they have something that makes them excited to wake up in the morning?
Do they feel connected to the places and communities around them?
And perhaps most importantly, do they recognize the life they’re living as one they actually wanted?
I don’t think those questions have simple answers.
And I certainly don’t think financial security is unimportant.
Money provides opportunities, independence, comfort, and the ability to care for ourselves and other people.
The freedom to pursue an unconventional life is often made possible by forms of stability that are easy to overlook.
But I also think there is a point at which the pursuit of security can become so consuming that we forget what we wanted that security for.
We spend years preparing to live.
We tell ourselves that once we’ve earned enough, accomplished enough, or reached the next milestone, we’ll finally have the freedom to do the things that matter to us.
And sometimes that future keeps moving further away.
There is always another expense, another responsibility, another reason to wait.
I wonder how many people arrive at a point of relative stability only to realize that they’ve become so accustomed to postponing their desires that they no longer know what they want.
That possibility frightens me more than the idea of taking an unconventional path.
Not because I think everyone should quit their jobs and move to the mountains.
But because I think it’s possible to become so focused on constructing a successful life that we forget to experience the one we’re already living.
At the same time, I don’t want to confuse spontaneity with purpose.
I’ve begun to recognize that constantly seeking the next experience can become its own form of avoidance.
There will always be another mountain, another trip, another project, another version of life that seems more exciting than the one directly in front of us.
And if we’re not careful, the pursuit of freedom can turn into an inability to be satisfied with anything.
I think there is a certain discipline required to appreciate the ordinary.
To find meaning in work that isn’t always exciting.
To maintain relationships when they’re inconvenient.
To commit to a project long enough to see what it might become.
To remain somewhere after the initial fascination has faded.
These things are not particularly romantic.
But I suspect they are part of what makes a genuinely fulfilling life possible.
I’ve always admired people who seem willing to take risks in pursuit of something they believe in.
But I’m beginning to admire another kind of courage as well.
The courage to choose something and stay with it.
To accept that every life involves limitations.
To stop imagining that fulfillment exists somewhere just beyond the next decision.
And to recognize that a meaningful life is not necessarily one in which we experience everything.
It may be one in which we learn to experience the things we’ve chosen more fully.
I think about this when I imagine my future.
There are so many different lives I can picture myself enjoying.
I can imagine working in the ski industry, traveling with filmmakers, and spending winters in the mountains.
I can imagine building a creative business, making photographs, telling stories, and developing projects that feel entirely my own.
I can imagine living near the ocean, sailing in the summer, and returning to the places that shaped my childhood.
I can also imagine wanting a home, a family, familiar people around me, and a degree of stability that makes the rest of those experiences possible.
For a long time, the existence of so many possibilities has made it difficult to know which direction to pursue.
But perhaps the goal isn’t to discover the one perfect version of life.
Perhaps it’s to build something that allows the different parts of ourselves to coexist.
To be ambitious without allowing ambition to consume us.
To value freedom without rejecting responsibility.
To pursue adventure without treating ordinary life as something to escape.
To create meaningful work without expecting every moment of it to feel inspiring.
And to recognize that choosing one path doesn’t necessarily mean abandoning everything we love about the others.
I think that’s what the romance of the unconventional life really represents to me.
Not a rejection of adulthood, responsibility, or the practical realities of the world.
But the possibility that we have more influence over the shape of our lives than we sometimes allow ourselves to believe.
We may not be able to control every circumstance.
We cannot guarantee that our careers will unfold as planned, that the places we love will remain unchanged, or that the opportunities available to us today will exist forever.
But we can question the assumptions that guide our decisions.
We can pay attention to what makes us feel genuinely alive.
We can recognize when we’re pursuing something because we want it and when we’re pursuing it because we’ve been taught that we should.
And we can try to build lives that reflect those distinctions.
I don’t know exactly what my life will look like in ten years.
I don’t know whether I’ll end up making films, running a creative business, living in a mountain town, or finding myself somewhere I haven’t even considered yet.
There is a part of me that finds that uncertainty exciting.
And another part that finds it terrifying.
I think both feelings are reasonable.
Because the freedom to choose your own path also means accepting that you might make the wrong choices.
That some things won’t work out.
That certain opportunities will pass.
And that there may never be a moment when you feel completely certain you’ve figured everything out.
But I’m beginning to think that certainty was never really the point.
I don’t want an unconventional life simply for the sake of being different.
I don’t want to spend my life chasing freedom so relentlessly that I become incapable of appreciating what I already have.
And I don’t want to mistake the appearance of an interesting life for the experience of actually living one.
I want to be curious.
I want to make things.
I want to work hard at something I care about.
I want to spend time in places that remind me how extraordinary the world can be.
I want relationships that are worth rearranging my plans for.
And I want enough independence to continue discovering what those things mean to me as I get older.
Maybe that life will look unconventional from the outside.
Maybe parts of it will look surprisingly ordinary.
I don’t think that distinction matters as much as I once believed.
Because perhaps the most romantic thing about an unconventional life isn’t the ability to escape expectations.
It’s the possibility of living without allowing those expectations to make all of our decisions for us.
To recognize that the world offers an extraordinary number of ways to exist within it, and that none of us are required to pursue the same definition of a life well lived.
And perhaps growing up isn’t the process of abandoning the lives we once dreamed about.
Maybe it’s learning how to build one that still feels like our own, even after we understand what it costs.

essays.title: In Pursuit of Something Real
essays.subtitle: On the places that shape us, the things we choose to value, and the search for a life that feels meaningful.

body.text: I think the older I get, the more I realize my life has been shaped less by accomplishments and more by environments. By mountains, oceans, storms, communities, long dinner tables, chairlifts, family traditions, and the kinds of people who dedicate themselves fully to the things they love. I think my values were formed there long before I even knew what values were.

I grew up between very different worlds. On one side there was the East Coast, with its old shore towns, family traditions, yacht clubs, and generations of history layered into the same streets, houses, and stories. Summers where cousins lived almost as siblings, where dinner stretched late into the night and every adult seemed larger than life when I was little. There was structure there, ambition, education, expectation. My family worked incredibly hard to build the life they gave me, and I’ve always carried a deep awareness of that privilege and responsibility.
But on the other side of my life, there were mountains.
And the mountains taught me entirely different lessons.

I didn’t grow up religious in the traditional sense. My dad used to joke that skiers don’t go to church on Sundays because skiing is church. At first it sounded funny, but as I got older I realized there was something deeply true about it. Some people find spirituality in buildings or rituals or scripture. I found it standing on ridgelines before sunrise, watching storms move through the Wasatch, hearing the silence that only exists in the mountains after heavy snowfall.
That became my compass.

Skiing shaped not only what I love, but how I see the world. Mountains humble you. They do not care how successful you are, how attractive you are, how much money you make, or how many people follow you online. Snow doesn’t respond to ego. Weather does not bend to ambition. In the mountains, reality becomes very simple very quickly. You learn respect. You learn awareness. You learn that nature is not something you conquer but something you move with.
I think that’s why authenticity matters so much to me.

I’ve always struggled with how performative modern life can feel. So much of the world now feels curated for appearance instead of meaning. People document moments before they even experience them. Everything becomes branding, status, optimization, networking. But the moments that have mattered most in my life have always been the least performative ones.
A freezing parking lot before dawn with close friends.
A powder day where nobody checks their phone for hours.
My family laughing around a dinner table.
Driving canyon roads while everyone else sleeps in the car.
Watching snow fall outside a cabin window late at night.
Those moments feel sacred to me because they’re real. Nobody’s trying to prove anything in those moments. Nobody’s selling a version of themselves. People are simply alive together.
And I think that’s ultimately what I value most in life: presence.

Real presence is becoming rare. Most people are distracted all the time by screens, by pressure, by insecurity, by the need to constantly present themselves to the world. But skiing, photography, filmmaking, travel, even long conversations with people I love, those are the things that force me back into the present moment. They remind me life is actually happening right now, not later when everything is more perfect.
That awareness also makes me deeply emotional about impermanence.

I think about time constantly. About how fast things change. Communities change. Mountains change. Families age. Friends move away. Places that once felt eternal quietly disappear or become unrecognizable. And maybe because I love places and people so deeply, I feel that loss very intensely.
I think that’s part of why storytelling matters so much to me too.

Photography and filmmaking are not just creative outlets for me. They’re acts of preservation. I want to capture how something felt before it vanishes. Not just the image itself, but the atmosphere. The emotion. The humanity inside it. I want to document ski culture because I believe there’s something deeply beautiful about communities built around shared passion and hardship and joy. I want to tell stories about places like Powder Mountain because places like that are increasingly rare, places where soul still matters more than status.
I think I’m constantly searching for soul in things.
In people.
In places.
In experiences.

I admire people who are deeply themselves. People who care passionately. People who dedicate their lives to something meaningful even if it isn’t glamorous. My mom embodies that to me completely. She is one of the strongest and most disciplined people I know, but what inspires me most is not just her success. It’s her consistency, her resilience, her refusal to stop growing. My dad taught me something equally important: that life should actually be lived. That joy matters. That passion matters. That mountains and adventure and community are not distractions from life but part of the point of it.
And I think those lessons created a tension in me that I still live with every day.

Part of me wants freedom endlessly. Winters chasing storms, creating films, living creatively, experiencing the world fully and emotionally. Another part of me understands responsibility, adulthood, career expectations, stability. I’m still trying to figure out how to balance those things without losing myself. But maybe balance isn’t something static. Maybe it’s something you continuously adjust to, like skiing difficult terrain, always moving, always responding.
At my core, I think I believe life is supposed to be felt deeply.

I don’t want to sleepwalk through existence chasing things I don’t actually care about. I don’t want to become so consumed by work or image or pressure that I stop noticing beauty. Because beauty is everywhere if you’re paying attention. In storms. In old family traditions. In exhausted laughter after long days. In mountains at dusk. In salt air during East Coast summers. In friendships built through shared experiences and hardship and adventure.
And honestly, I think my greatest fear is losing touch with that sense of wonder.
Because wonder is what makes life meaningful.
Not achievement alone.
Not status.
Not money.

Those things matter to some extent, of course. But I’ve met enough successful people to know accomplishment without soul eventually becomes emptiness. The people I admire most are people who remain connected to nature, to community, to curiosity, to passion, to love.
That’s the kind of person I hope to become.
Someone who notices things.
Someone who preserves beauty.
Someone who values experiences over appearances.
Someone who remains emotionally alive even when the world encourages numbness.
Someone who understands that mountains are not just landscapes but teachers.

Because skiing taught me almost everything I believe about life. Respect uncertainty. Stay adaptable. Commit fully. Trust instinct. Remain humble. Be present. Some days will break your heart. Some days will feel transcendent. Most disappear faster than you expect. And the entire point is to experience them completely while they’re here.
I think that’s my philosophy more than anything else.
To live fully.
To love places and people deeply.
To stay curious.
To protect what is meaningful.
And to never lose the ability to stand in awe of the world.

essays.title: So You Think You Can Fly
essays.subtitle: On the pursuit of adrenaline, the psychology of fear, and our obsession with feeling alive

body.text: When I was a little kid, whenever someone asked me what superpower I would choose if I could have any in the world, I always had the same answer: I wanted to fly. Not to be invisible, not to read minds, or to have superhuman strength. I just wanted to fly. There was something about the idea of being weightless, of escaping gravity and moving freely through the air, that fascinated me. Looking back, I don’t think that desire ever really went away. I think I just found different ways to chase it.
And I don’t think I’m alone in that.

Across the world, people dedicate their lives to sports that, in one way or another, allow us to experience something remarkably close to flight. Skiers launch themselves off cliffs, snowboarders float through the air, skateboarders throw themselves down massive gaps, mountain bikers fly over jumps, and surfers ride walls of moving water. From the outside, these pursuits might seem reckless, unnecessary, or even irrational. Why would anyone willingly put themselves in a situation where they could get seriously hurt, or worse, just for a few seconds of excitement? But I think anyone who has experienced that feeling understands that there is something much deeper happening. It’s not simply about getting air or chasing an adrenaline rush. It’s about fear, freedom, human potential, and the almost indescribable feeling of being completely alive.

One of the most fascinating aspects of action sports is our complicated relationship with fear. As human beings, we are biologically programmed to protect ourselves. Fear is a survival mechanism designed to keep us away from danger. Yet, in action sports, we deliberately seek out situations that activate those instincts. We stand at the top of cliffs, look down at enormous jumps, or paddle into waves that could easily overpower us. Our hearts start racing, our hands shake, and every instinct in our bodies tells us to reconsider what we’re about to do. And then, despite all of that, we commit.

There’s something incredibly powerful about the moment when you overcome that hesitation. When you do something that genuinely scares you and come out the other side, you experience a kind of satisfaction that is difficult to replicate in everyday life. It’s not just relief that you survived. It’s the realization that you were capable of something you previously believed might be beyond your limits. Something that seemed impossible suddenly becomes possible, and that changes the way you perceive yourself.

I think this is one of the reasons action sports can become so consuming. Every time you push past a boundary, you begin to question where the next one lies. The jump that once terrified you becomes comfortable. The line you once thought was impossible becomes something you know you can ski. Your understanding of your own capabilities expands, and naturally, you begin to wonder what else you can accomplish. How far can you push yourself? What are the actual limits of the human body and mind? And how much of what we consider impossible is simply something we haven’t attempted yet?

From a psychological perspective, there’s something particularly interesting about the reward we experience after confronting fear. Adrenaline heightens our awareness and prepares our bodies to respond to danger, while the brain’s reward systems can reinforce experiences associated with excitement, accomplishment, and relief. When we voluntarily enter a frightening situation and successfully navigate it, that experience can create an extraordinary sense of confidence and satisfaction. It’s almost as though we’ve proven something fundamental to ourselves: that we are capable of handling more than we thought.

But that reward also creates an interesting paradox. The more comfortable we become with risk, the further we may feel compelled to push it. Sometimes the experience doesn’t go according to plan. We fall, crash, break bones, or find ourselves in situations that remind us just how vulnerable we really are. And yet, for many athletes, those experiences don’t necessarily eliminate the desire to continue. Sometimes they intensify the determination to improve, to understand what went wrong, and to try again.

There is, of course, a fine line between courage and recklessness. The consequences of these sports are real, and not every risk is worth taking. But I think what makes this relationship with danger so fascinating is that most athletes aren’t necessarily chasing death. They’re chasing the extraordinary intensity of life that comes from confronting something uncertain. There’s a difference between wanting to die and wanting to experience something so powerful that it reminds you what it means to be alive.

And yet, I think it would be a mistake to define action sports entirely through adrenaline and danger. Because there’s another side to these experiences that is almost the complete opposite of fear. It’s a feeling of peace, weightlessness, and connection that can be just as addictive as the adrenaline itself.

For me, skiing is one of the clearest examples of this. There’s a particular feeling that comes from skiing deep, untouched powder that is nearly impossible to explain to someone who hasn’t experienced it. The snow seems to absorb everything around you. The sound of your skis becomes muffled, your movements become fluid, and rather than feeling like you’re forcing your way down a mountain, it almost feels as though you’re floating through it. You aren’t thinking about what happened yesterday or what you need to do tomorrow. You’re simply there, completely immersed in the moment.

Surfers experience something similar when they find themselves perfectly positioned on a wave. For a few seconds, they’re moving in harmony with an enormous force of nature, responding instinctively to the water beneath them. Snowboarders carving through fresh snow, mountain bikers flowing down a trail, and skateboarders landing a trick effortlessly can all experience their own versions of this sensation. Different sports, different environments, but something fundamentally similar connects them.

Psychologists have a name for this kind of experience: flow. It’s a state of complete immersion in an activity, where attention becomes so focused that self-consciousness and the normal perception of time can seem to disappear. Flow often occurs when the challenge of an activity is closely matched to a person’s abilities, requiring enough concentration that there is little room for anything else. I think this concept helps explain why action sports can feel so therapeutic. In a world where we’re constantly distracted, overthinking, worrying, and anticipating the future, these sports force us into the present.

The more I think about this feeling, the more fascinated I become by the psychology behind it. Because what if the reason we dedicate so much of our lives to these sports has less to do with adrenaline than we think? What if we’re actually chasing a particular state of consciousness, one that allows us to experience the world, ourselves, and our own capabilities in a way that everyday life rarely permits?

Hungarian-American psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi spent much of his career investigating a similar question. He wanted to understand what makes certain experiences so deeply rewarding that people pursue them for no external reason at all. Through his research with artists, musicians, athletes, rock climbers, and people engaged in challenging activities, he identified a psychological state he called flow. What fascinated him was that people from completely different backgrounds described remarkably similar experiences when they became fully absorbed in something they loved. Their awareness of time changed, their self-consciousness faded, and the distinction between thinking and doing seemed to disappear. They weren’t necessarily pursuing money, recognition, or some tangible reward. The experience itself was the reward.

Csikszentmihalyi described this as an autotelic experience, meaning an activity that is intrinsically rewarding rather than simply a means to some other end. I think that distinction is incredibly important when trying to understand action sports. Because while competitions, sponsorships, recognition, and progression are certainly part of these sports, I don’t think they explain why so many of us fell in love with them in the first place. Before there were cameras, competitions, or anyone watching, there was simply the feeling. The sensation of moving through the world in a way that made us want to do it again and again, even if nobody else ever knew we’d done it.

One of the central ideas in Csikszentmihalyi’s research is the relationship between challenge and skill. Flow is most likely to emerge when an activity demands enough of our abilities to require complete concentration, but not so much that we become entirely overwhelmed. If something is too easy, we become bored. If it’s too difficult, we may become anxious or discouraged. But somewhere between those two extremes exists this extraordinary psychological state where our abilities and the demands of the moment seem to align.

I think this explains something fundamental about progression in action sports. As we improve, the challenges that once required our complete attention gradually become familiar. A jump that once demanded every ounce of courage and concentration eventually becomes routine. A difficult line becomes something we can navigate almost instinctively. And while there’s satisfaction in that improvement, the experience may no longer command our attention in quite the same way. So we seek out new challenges, not necessarily because we need more danger, but because we want to rediscover that level of complete engagement.
Maybe part of what we interpret as an addiction to adrenaline is actually a desire to return to flow.

But what makes this state particularly interesting is that it involves a strange relationship with control. Csikszentmihalyi identified a sense of control as one of the characteristics of flow, yet that doesn’t necessarily mean having complete control over the situation. Instead, it can mean feeling capable of responding to whatever the experience demands. A skier cannot control the mountain, just as a surfer cannot control the ocean. But through experience, instinct, and skill, they can learn to move with these forces rather than constantly fighting against them.

And perhaps that’s why the sensation can feel so much like flying. You’re not necessarily escaping gravity or overcoming nature. You’re becoming so completely synchronized with your environment that the forces acting upon you no longer feel like obstacles. They become part of the experience itself.

Another fascinating characteristic of flow is what psychologists describe as the merging of action and awareness. Normally, we tend to experience ourselves as conscious observers directing our own movements. We think about what we’re going to do, make decisions, evaluate our actions, and constantly adjust. But during flow, that separation can seem to disappear. Our movements become instinctive. Decisions happen without the same degree of deliberate thought. We stop consciously directing every action and begin simply responding.

Anyone who has experienced a perfect powder run knows how strange and incredible this can feel. You’re still making countless adjustments, reading the terrain, shifting your weight, and responding to the snow beneath you. But you aren’t consciously thinking through every movement. Your body seems to know what to do before your mind has time to explain it. What would normally require concentration begins to feel effortless, even though the activity itself may be incredibly demanding.

I think this is where the almost spiritual quality of action sports begins to make sense. Csikszentmihalyi also observed that people experiencing flow often report a temporary loss of self-consciousness. This doesn’t mean losing awareness of their surroundings. In fact, their attention may be more focused than ever. What disappears is the constant internal commentary that usually accompanies our lives. The part of our minds that worries about how we look, what other people think, whether we’re succeeding, or what we should be doing instead.
For a brief moment, the ego seems to get out of the way.

And there’s something incredibly freeing about that. So much of everyday life is spent thinking about ourselves, our responsibilities, our insecurities, our futures, and the endless expectations we place on our own lives. But when you’re completely immersed in a wave, a mountain, or a jump, there simply isn’t room for all of that. Your attention is occupied by the experience directly in front of you.
The past becomes irrelevant. The future temporarily disappears. All that exists is the present moment.

There’s another psychological dimension to this that I find especially compelling: our relationship with fear and mortality. Fear is generally understood as something unpleasant, an emotion we should avoid whenever possible. But when we voluntarily confront a challenge that scares us, fear can take on a different meaning. It becomes part of an experience that may ultimately leave us feeling more confident, capable, and alive.

Of course, this doesn’t mean that greater danger automatically creates greater fulfillment. Research on extreme sports suggests that participants have a wide variety of motivations, and many approach risk with careful preparation, discipline, and respect rather than recklessness. But I think there is something psychologically significant about choosing to confront uncertainty. When we place ourselves in a situation that demands our complete attention, the ordinary distractions of life lose their importance. The consequences of our decisions become immediate and tangible.

Maybe that’s one reason these experiences can make us feel so intensely alive. They temporarily strip life down to something incredibly simple. There is no room for pretending, procrastinating, or worrying about things that don’t matter in that moment. You have to be there, fully and completely, because your immediate reality demands it.

This also raises a more complicated question about the pursuit of human potential. Why are we so fascinated by discovering the limits of what we’re capable of? Why does accomplishing something difficult so often make us want to attempt something even harder?

Csikszentmihalyi’s work offers one possible explanation. As our abilities develop, we often need increasingly complex challenges to experience the same level of engagement. Growth and flow can become connected in a kind of ongoing cycle. We develop skills to meet a challenge, experience the satisfaction of using those skills, and then seek new challenges that demand further growth.

In action sports, we can see this process unfolding across entire generations. Tricks that once seemed unimaginable become standard. Lines that were once considered impossible are eventually skied. Athletes continually redefine what can be accomplished on a skateboard, surfboard, snowboard, bike, or pair of skis. And every time someone expands those boundaries, they change what the next generation believes is possible.

But perhaps the most meaningful form of progression isn’t always about going bigger or doing something more dangerous. Sometimes it’s about developing a deeper understanding of the experience itself. Learning to move more naturally, to read the terrain more intuitively, to make better decisions, or to find satisfaction in something that doesn’t need to impress anyone else. This is where I think the relationship between action sports and nature becomes especially important. Mountains, oceans, and other natural environments are constantly changing. No two powder runs are exactly alike. No two waves break in precisely the same way. Even when we return to the same place, the experience is never entirely identical.

That unpredictability creates endless opportunities for learning, adaptation, and complete engagement. It also reminds us that no matter how skilled we become, there will always be forces beyond our control. Nature demands both confidence and humility. It gives us the opportunity to experience extraordinary freedom, but it also reminds us of our own vulnerability.

And maybe that’s part of the beauty of it. We’re not conquering the mountain or defeating the ocean. At our best, we’re learning how to exist within them, even if only for a few extraordinary moments.

What I find most interesting about Csikszentmihalyi’s research is that flow isn’t exclusive to action sports. People can experience it through music, art, writing, science, and countless other pursuits. The underlying psychology is not necessarily about danger or physical intensity. It’s about becoming so deeply engaged in something meaningful and challenging that the activity temporarily consumes our entire awareness.

But action sports offer a particularly physical expression of that experience. We don’t just think our way into flow. We feel it through our bodies, through gravity, speed, movement, snow, water, and air. The experience is simultaneously psychological and physical, something happening both inside us and in the world around us.

And perhaps that helps explain why it can be so difficult to describe. We’re trying to put words to an experience defined, in part, by the temporary disappearance of the very thoughts and internal dialogue we normally use to understand ourselves.
There’s something beautifully contradictory about that.

We spend so much of our lives trying to gain control, understand ourselves, and make sense of everything around us. Yet some of our most meaningful experiences happen when we stop consciously analyzing everything and allow ourselves to become completely immersed in what we’re doing.

Maybe that’s what we’re really searching for when we chase these moments. Not simply excitement, not simply danger, and not even necessarily the accomplishment of something difficult. Maybe we’re searching for those rare experiences where the distance between ourselves and the world seems to disappear.
Where movement becomes instinct, fear becomes focus, and the boundaries between our bodies and our surroundings begin to feel less distinct.
Where, for a few fleeting seconds, we stop thinking about what it means to be alive.
And simply experience it.
There’s something almost spiritual about that.

When you’re skiing a perfect line or riding an incredible wave, you aren’t trying to solve all the problems in your life. You’re not worrying about how other people perceive you. You’re not thinking about responsibilities, expectations, or everything you wish you could change. For those few moments, all of that disappears. Your mind and body are working together so instinctively that the experience feels almost effortless. It’s a kind of freedom that can be difficult to find anywhere else.

What I find especially fascinating is that this peaceful feeling and the intense adrenaline of danger can exist within the exact same sports, sometimes even within the same run. One moment, you’re standing above a line with your heart pounding, questioning whether you should commit. The next, you’re moving through the terrain with complete confidence, experiencing an almost meditative sense of clarity. Fear and freedom, two emotions that seem completely opposed, somehow become intertwined.

Perhaps that’s part of what makes these experiences so powerful. In everyday life, we often associate freedom with comfort, security, and having control over our surroundings. But in action sports, some of the greatest feelings of freedom occur when we surrender a certain amount of that control. We cannot control gravity. We cannot control the ocean. We cannot completely predict the conditions of a mountain. We can prepare, practice, develop our skills, and learn to understand these environments, but ultimately, we have to work with forces much larger than ourselves.
In a strange way, that surrender can be liberating.

There’s also something meaningful about the relationship between action sports and the natural world. Skiing, surfing, snowboarding, and mountain biking allow us to interact with landscapes in ways that go far beyond simply observing them. We aren’t just looking at mountains or watching waves break from the shore. We’re moving through them, responding to their shapes, rhythms, and energy. The terrain becomes something we experience physically rather than just visually. Over time, that relationship can create a profound sense of connection and respect for the environments that make these experiences possible.

Maybe this is why so many people who dedicate their lives to these sports struggle to explain what they mean to them. It’s easy to describe the adrenaline. It’s easy to show someone a massive cliff drop or an impressive trick and explain why it looks exciting. But it’s much harder to communicate the feeling of floating through snow, of being perfectly in sync with a wave, or of landing something you’ve spent years imagining. These experiences are intensely physical, but their impact often extends far beyond the moment itself.

They change how we see ourselves. They teach us about fear, failure, patience, confidence, and resilience. They remind us that our bodies are capable of extraordinary things, but also that we are fragile. They show us how rewarding it can be to push beyond what feels comfortable, while simultaneously teaching us that some boundaries deserve respect.
And perhaps most importantly, they give us moments that make us look back on our lives and feel like we truly lived them.

I think that’s ultimately what we’re chasing. Not just adrenaline, not just progression, and not even necessarily the feeling of flight itself. We’re chasing experiences that pull us completely out of the ordinary. Moments so intense, beautiful, frightening, or freeing that they become impossible to forget. Moments that remind us there is more to being alive than simply moving through the routines of everyday existence.

As a kid, I thought flying would mean escaping gravity, lifting off the ground, and moving through the sky without limitations. Now I think flying can mean something much more complicated. Sometimes it’s the few seconds spent suspended in the air above a jump. Sometimes it’s the terrifying commitment of dropping into something that scares you. Sometimes it’s floating through deep powder, completely absorbed in the rhythm of the mountain. And sometimes it’s simply the realization that you’ve done something you never thought you could do.

Maybe the reason we keep coming back to these sports is that they give us access to a feeling we’re constantly searching for in other parts of our lives: the feeling of being entirely present, entirely free, and undeniably alive.
Maybe we’ve never really stopped wanting to fly.
We’ve just learned that there are different ways to leave the ground.
And maybe the question was never whether we could fly in the first place.
Maybe the real question is why we need to.

essays.title: The Fragility of Extraordinary Things
essays.subtitle: On the inheritance of ambition, the limits of the human body, and the complicated ways we learn what it means to live.

body.text: I come from a family of people who have spent much of their lives trying to understand what human beings are capable of.

Some pursued that question through science. Others through endurance, adventure, art, or the relentless desire to see what existed beyond the world they already knew. Often, they pursued it through all of those things at once.

For a long time, I understood their accomplishments as evidence of something almost limitless about human potential. I grew up surrounded by stories of extraordinary people doing extraordinary things, and I think I inherited the assumption that life was supposed to be approached with curiosity, ambition, and a willingness to challenge what seemed possible.
But as I’ve gotten older, I’ve begun to understand another side of that inheritance.

I’ve watched people who spent their lives studying the human body become vulnerable to the very systems they worked to understand. I’ve watched extraordinary athletes lose the freedom to move. I’ve watched the responsibilities of love become complicated by illness, guilt, exhaustion, and grief.

And I’ve begun to wonder whether the most important lessons my family has taught me have less to do with what human beings can accomplish than with what remains when accomplishment is no longer possible.
My maternal grandparents, Harriet and Robert Baker, came from backgrounds far removed from the academic and scientific worlds in which they would eventually build their careers.

My grandfather grew up on a farm in Iowa. My grandmother grew up in Newark, New Jersey, the daughter of Celia and Benjamin Arons, in a Jewish community where her curiosity about science was apparent long before she could have imagined making a career out of it.
When she was a little girl, she asked her parents for a chemistry set for her birthday.
It was an unusual request for a young girl at the time, and her parents reluctantly agreed, on the condition that she conduct her experiments in the basement.
I only learned that story recently, reading a memorial biography my grandfather wrote after her death.
I love the image of my grandmother as a young girl, experimenting in the basement of her family home, already fascinated by questions she would spend the rest of her life trying to answer.

I have photographs of her from that period of her life, one at twelve and another at fifteen. In one, she stands outside wearing a long coat and a hat, smiling at the camera. In another, she poses with her hands on her hips, wearing shorts and a sleeveless blouse.
I look at those photographs and try to reconcile the girl in them with the woman I knew.

The grandmother who taught me card games and how to use a sewing machine. The woman who could recognize almost any bird by its call. The scientist who dedicated decades to understanding the brain. The person whose illness would eventually change so much of what made her recognizable to the people who loved her.
All of those versions of her existed within one life.
And I think that’s something we rarely stop to consider about the people closest to us.

We know them through the relatively small portion of their lives that overlaps with our own. We inherit their stories, their habits, and their influence, but entire decades of their existence remain almost unimaginable to us.
My grandparents went on to become accomplished neuroscientists, dedicating their careers to studying the brain and nervous system.

My grandmother earned advanced degrees in pharmacology and spent roughly forty years conducting research at Weill Cornell Medical College and the Burke Neurological Institute. According to the memorial my grandfather wrote, she published 140 scientific papers and was cited in more than 5,400 others.
Her work focused on the olfactory system, dopamine-producing neurons, and the search for alternative neuronal sources relevant to Parkinson’s disease.

My grandfather became a professor and researcher at NYU’s medical school, studying the neural systems responsible for movement, balance, and coordination. His research investigated how the brain allows us to perform actions that most of us never consciously consider, from stabilizing our vision while moving our heads to adapting the complex movements of our bodies.

I find it extraordinary that two people who began their lives in such different circumstances would come together and devote themselves to understanding one of the most complicated things in the known universe.
The human brain.
But what I find equally interesting is that neither of them seemed content to understand life exclusively through academic study.
They were also athletes, travelers, naturalists, artists, and adventurers.

Their scientific careers took them around the world. They traveled to places as distant as Antarctica, Japan, France, Africa, and the Himalayas, building friendships and professional relationships within an international community of researchers.
My mother and aunt grew up in a family where travel was often intertwined with scientific work, and where curiosity about the world was not limited to the laboratory.

My mother spent part of her early childhood living in Japan, where she learned to speak Japanese, and later spent time living in France. She still speaks French, and throughout my childhood, whenever it was time for us to leave somewhere, she would say the same thing.
On y va.
Let’s go.

It’s such a small detail, something I’ve heard thousands of times without giving it much thought. But I love the idea that an experience my mother had as a young child in another country became part of the ordinary language of my own childhood.

I think family history often survives in ways like that. Not necessarily through the stories we consciously preserve, but through the habits, expressions, and ways of seeing the world that are passed down almost without our noticing.

My grandfather ran marathons and competed in Ironman triathlons around the world, continuing to challenge himself physically long after most people would have considered slowing down. My grandmother was a marathon runner too.
My mother inherited that passion, and she and my grandfather competed in endurance events together, including the Ironman World Championship in Hawaii.
When I was little, my brother and I crossed the finish line with my mother.
I don’t think I could have understood the significance of that moment at the time.

An Ironman involves swimming 2.4 miles, cycling 112 miles, and then running a full marathon. It’s an almost absurd undertaking when you stop to think about it. Hours upon hours of physical exertion, training, discomfort, and uncertainty, all in pursuit of a finish line that holds no practical necessity.
And yet, for my family, experiences like that were never simply about athletic achievement.
They were expressions of a particular relationship with life.
My parents’ honeymoon was hardly conventional. They traveled with my maternal grandparents and aunt to the Himalayas, climbing in the mountains near Everest, and also spent time surfing in Bali.
I love that detail about my family’s history.
There is something wonderfully unconventional about beginning a marriage by bringing your parents and sister into an adventure on the other side of the world.

My grandfather recently told me more about that trip. While climbing toward Kala Patthar in Nepal, my mother and grandmother had to turn back because of altitude sickness. My father, grandfather, and aunt continued to the top, waiting for the clouds to clear so they could see the extraordinary landscape surrounding Everest.

And among all the things my grandfather remembers about standing in one of the most remarkable places on Earth, he also remembers my father making some ridiculous comment about a boiled egg my aunt had brought along.
I love that.
Not just the summit or the view, but the fact that a joke about a boiled egg survived decades of extraordinary experiences and somehow made its way back to me over dinner.

I recently learned another story about my mother and aunt in their twenties. When my grandparents decided to spend a month traveling through Africa, both of their daughters left their jobs and joined them. They explored the Serengeti and other parts of the continent together, choosing an experience with their family over the professional routines they had already begun to establish.
I had never heard that story before, but something about it felt completely unsurprising.
Adventure was not necessarily an escape from responsibility or a reward reserved for the end of a successful career. It was part of life itself.
The pursuit of knowledge and the pursuit of experience were not separate ambitions.
They belonged together.
And I think that understanding shaped me long before I was old enough to recognize it.

I grew up believing that curiosity should extend beyond the classroom, that physical movement could be a form of discovery, and that the world was something to participate in rather than simply observe.
But some of my strongest memories of my grandparents have very little to do with their accomplishments.

For much of my early childhood, they were still working as professors and living primarily in White Plains, New York, where my mother and aunt had grown up after spending their earlier years in New York City. As I got older, my grandparents spent more time at their home in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, on Cape Cod.
For roughly two weeks every summer, that house became part of my world.
I remember the koi pond, the gardens, my grandfather’s woodshop, and the beaches where we spent hours exploring the rocks and shallow water.

My grandfather had spent much of his scientific career studying the nervous systems of animals, including fish, and I think that curiosity about living things found its way into even the simplest activities we did together.

We would take old wooden paint stirrers from his workshop and turn them into makeshift fishing lines, crushing snails with rocks to use as bait while we tried to catch crabs and little fish along the shoreline.
I think about that now and realize how much those afternoons reflected the environment I was growing up in.
There was always something to investigate, something to build, something to figure out.
The natural world wasn’t simply scenery. It was something worth understanding.

Some summers involved taking the ferry to Martha’s Vineyard, where cycling was part of the adventure. My family’s idea of a day exploring an island could involve an extraordinarily long bike ride, which probably says as much about the people who raised me as any of their professional achievements.
But when I think about my grandmother, I don’t immediately think about her scientific accomplishments.
I think about birds.

For as long as I can remember, she seemed to know every bird that appeared outside. She could recognize them by sight, identify their calls, and imitate so many of their sounds that it sometimes seemed as though she spoke a language the rest of us had never bothered to learn.
Her curiosity about living things didn’t end when she left the laboratory.
It followed her into the garden, onto the beaches, and into the ordinary moments of everyday life.
She was also an extraordinary gardener, a wonderful cook and baker, and a talented seamstress.

I’ve always found it a little funny that someone with the last name Baker happened to be so good at baking. She was the person who first inspired my own love of it. We would go apple picking together and then come home to make homemade applesauce, spending afternoons in the kitchen doing something that felt entirely ordinary at the time.

She made dresses for my mother and aunt when they were young, and she taught me how to use her sewing machine. We even took a sewing class together once. I still have and use many of her sewing supplies, something that has become increasingly meaningful to me as I’ve grown older and developed my own love of making things.
At Woods Hole, we would collect shells along the beaches, particularly Racing Beach, and she would preserve them and turn them into jewelry and other small creations.
I love that she was a scientist who also seemed to find endless satisfaction in making things with her hands.
She understood the world through research and observation, but she also engaged with it through craft, gardening, cooking, and art.
And I think those forms of curiosity are much more closely related than we often acknowledge.
Science asks us to look carefully at the world and try to understand what we see.
Art asks us to look carefully at the world and find a way to express what it means to us.
Both begin with attention.
My grandmother was also a writer.
Recently, while going through old emails, I found a message she sent me in January 2016, when I was still in school.
She was congratulating me on an essay I had written about To Kill a Mockingbird, which had apparently earned me a visit to the principal’s office for recognition.
She told me that she enjoyed writing too, and that she hoped someday to write a book about her experience living with Parkinson’s disease.
I had forgotten about that email.
Reading it now, after everything that happened, I find myself wishing I could ask her so many questions.
What would she have written?
