Would she have approached the experience as a scientist, trying to understand the biological processes unfolding within her own body? Or would she have written about the emotional experience of slowly losing abilities she had spent her life taking for granted?
Perhaps both.
I think about the fact that she was encouraging me to write while carrying an extraordinary story of her own, one she hoped she might someday have the opportunity to tell.
And now, years later, I’m sitting here trying to tell part of that story myself.
My mother became one of the clearest examples of the philosophy my grandparents passed down.

She built a demanding professional career while continuing to pursue endurance sports, skiing, and adventure. I have always admired her discipline, but I think what has impressed me most is her ability to sustain that discipline across so many different parts of life.
There is something remarkable about people who refuse to accept that being accomplished in one area means abandoning curiosity in another.
And yet, I think growing up around that kind of achievement can create a complicated understanding of success.
When extraordinary effort becomes familiar, it can begin to feel ordinary.
You develop a sense that you should always be doing more, learning more, becoming more, pushing further.
That ambition can be an extraordinary gift.
But it can also make it difficult to understand your own worth when you’re not accomplishing something.
I think this is a tension I’ve inherited as much as any love of mountains or adventure.

Part of me believes deeply in discipline, responsibility, and the satisfaction of working toward something difficult. Another part of me resists the idea that a meaningful life can be measured through achievement alone.
And perhaps that contradiction has become more apparent because of what happened to my grandparents.
My grandmother developed Parkinson’s disease, an illness that progressively affected her ability to move and, in her later years, profoundly changed her cognitive and emotional life.

There is a particularly painful irony in the fact that she had spent so much of her career studying the nervous system, including dopamine-related processes and research relevant to Parkinson’s disease.
In the memorial he wrote after her death, my grandfather explained that she had recognized the symptoms in herself and diagnosed her own Parkinson’s disease in 1997.
She had spent years contributing to scientific research that sought to understand the very systems that were beginning to fail her.
But knowledge is not immunity.
Understanding the mechanisms of a disease does not necessarily make someone less vulnerable to it.
And perhaps that’s one of the most unsettling truths about the human condition.
We can devote entire lifetimes to understanding something and still be unable to control it.
For years, my grandfather cared for my grandmother as her illness progressed.
I think there is a kind of devotion in caregiving that rarely receives the recognition given to more visible forms of achievement.
It doesn’t come with medals or publications. There is no finish line, no clear measure of progress, and often no promise that tomorrow will be easier than today.
It is repetitive, exhausting, emotionally complicated work.
And it is work that can fundamentally alter the relationship between two people.
Someone who was once a partner in adventure, conversation, and shared independence becomes increasingly dependent on the person who loves them.
My grandfather has always called my grandmother Chief.

For as long as I’ve known them, that’s simply who she was. Whatever Chief wanted, Chief got. There was something wonderfully affectionate about the way he said it, as though he had accepted long ago that she was in charge and wouldn’t have wanted it any other way.
Even as her Parkinson’s progressed and she began losing so much of the independence and cognitive clarity that had defined her earlier life, she remained Chief.
And even now, after her death, that’s still how he refers to her.
I think there is something deeply moving about that.
Their relationship had been built over decades of shared work, travel, family, and adventure. As her illness progressed, so many of the things they once enjoyed together became impossible.
But the affection with which he spoke about her never seemed to depend on what she was still capable of doing.
I imagine there must have been moments of tenderness, frustration, grief, and exhaustion that are almost impossible to communicate to someone who has not lived through them.
And I think the experience challenges many of our conventional ideas about strength.
Sometimes strength is not climbing a mountain or completing a race.
Sometimes it is getting up the next morning and continuing to care for someone whose world has become smaller, even as your own world changes around that responsibility.
But then, in a cruel turn of circumstances, my grandfather’s life changed almost instantaneously.

One summer, while cycling near Woods Hole on Cape Cod with my mother, a truck approached from behind. My grandfather braked and went over his handlebars, suffering a catastrophic injury that left him with extensive paralysis.
He had spent decades studying how the nervous system coordinates movement.
He had run marathons, completed Ironman triathlons, and traveled across the world in pursuit of physical and intellectual challenges.
And in a matter of seconds, much of his ability to move independently was gone.
I have thought about the contrast between those two versions of his life many times.
The man who could swim miles, cycle more than a hundred miles, and run a marathon in a single day suddenly faced limitations that no amount of determination could simply overcome.
Through rehabilitation, persistence, and an extraordinary understanding of his own condition, he regained some movement. But the injury permanently changed his independence.
He could no longer care for my grandmother as he once had.
And suddenly, both of my grandparents needed extensive care.
I think about what that must have meant for my mother and aunt.

The people who had taught them to be strong, ambitious, capable, and independent were now confronting circumstances in which those qualities could not restore the lives they had known. My mother had spent years following in their footsteps, professionally in her own way and physically through the endurance sports and adventures they shared.
She had learned from people who seemed to approach every challenge as something to be understood, worked through, or overcome.
But what happens when a problem cannot be solved through discipline?
What happens when effort is not enough?
What happens when love cannot reverse what has happened?
I think one of the most difficult aspects of caring for someone is the guilt that can accompany it.
The feeling that you should be doing more, that there must be another solution, another sacrifice, another way to make things better.
And when the people who need you are your parents, I imagine that responsibility becomes entangled with a lifetime of gratitude, expectation, and love.
My mother has carried that guilt in ways I’ve become increasingly aware of as I’ve gotten older.
I don’t think it’s possible to understand another person’s experience of that responsibility completely, especially when you’re witnessing it as their child.
But I have begun to recognize that love doesn’t always give us the ability to fix what is wrong.
Sometimes it simply means remaining present through circumstances that have no satisfying resolution.
My grandmother passed away in May 2023, at the age of eighty-two.
My grandfather wrote the memorial biography that I recently found among our family’s records.
He described her scientific accomplishments, her love of birdwatching and gardening, her marathon running, her sewing, her cooking, and her passion for collecting shells and sea glass.
But what struck me most was how he described her as a person.
Not simply as a scientist or an athlete, but as a woman with an extraordinary enthusiasm for life, someone whose generosity and curiosity extended into almost everything she did.
He ended by writing about how deeply she would be missed.
A lifetime of shared experience, condensed into a few paragraphs.
I think about how difficult that must have been to write.
How do you summarize someone you have spent sixty years loving?
How do you choose which details matter when almost every part of your life has been shaped by their presence?
And how do you begin to describe the absence of someone who has been beside you for so long?
My grandfather is still here, but his life is profoundly different from the one he once knew.

And I think one of the hardest things for me to reconcile is what it means for someone whose identity was so deeply connected to movement and independence to continue living with such severe physical limitations.
We often speak about the importance of the mind as though it exists separately from the body.
We celebrate intelligence, creativity, consciousness, and the extraordinary things human beings are capable of imagining.
But our ability to experience the world depends so intimately on our physical existence.
To walk outside. To climb a staircase. To swim. To ride a bicycle. To travel independently. To reach for something without thinking about the movement required.
These are things most of us take for granted precisely because we can do them without much thought.
Yet for someone who loses that freedom, the ordinary physical world can become a place of extraordinary obstacles.
I think about this when I ski.
The feeling of moving through deep snow, of responding instinctively to terrain, of allowing my body to make hundreds of small adjustments without conscious instruction.
I think about the freedom of movement and the strange satisfaction of being physically capable of responding to the world around me.
And I wonder whether I would appreciate those experiences in quite the same way if I hadn’t witnessed what happens when that freedom is taken away.
I don’t think the lesson is that we should live recklessly because life is short.
If anything, my family’s history has taught me how real the consequences of physical risk can be.
But it has also taught me that the ability to participate in life is not guaranteed.
And that awareness creates a kind of urgency.
Not necessarily to accomplish more.
But to experience more consciously.
To recognize the extraordinary privilege of being able to move through the world under our own power.
There is another part of my maternal family’s story that has made me think differently about how people respond to loss.
My aunt Jessica, my mother’s younger sister, is an artist.

She spent much of her creative life in Brooklyn before making her home in Woodstock, New York, with her husband, Ed Elefterion, a theater director, educator, and musician who creates music under the name Ed Charles.
Jessica’s work has long explored impermanence, memory, and the transformation of ordinary materials.

Years before my grandmother died, she was making prints on fallen leaves collected from the streets and parks of Brooklyn. She understood that the leaves would eventually decompose, and that their gradual disappearance was not a failure of the artwork but part of its meaning.
I find that idea incredibly beautiful.
The materials were never intended to last forever.
Their impermanence was precisely what made them worth noticing.

After my grandmother’s death, Jessica created artwork using objects that had belonged to her, including playing cards, shells, and other fragments of the collections she had accumulated over the years.
What makes that work especially personal to me is that I remember the cards.

My grandmother loved playing games, and I spent countless hours playing gin rummy with her throughout my childhood. She taught me other card games too, and those afternoons became part of the ordinary familiarity of being her granddaughter.
As her illness progressed and her cognitive world became increasingly difficult to understand, she continued handling playing cards, sometimes tearing them into pieces.
And now those same objects have become part of my aunt’s art.
I find something almost unbearably moving about that.

An ordinary deck of cards that once represented afternoons spent playing games with my grandmother became something she held onto as her world changed, and eventually something my aunt used to express the grief of losing her.
I don’t know that there is a more honest representation of memory.
We cannot always restore the things we’ve lost. Sometimes all we can do is gather what remains and try to make something meaningful from it.
Jessica also created the urn that now holds my grandmother’s ashes.
It is a colorful wooden box decorated with shells, pieces of sea glass, and images of birds taken from the cards my grandmother loved.
When I look at it, I recognize so many parts of the woman I knew.
The shells from the beaches.
The birds she could identify by sound.
The cards she held in her hands.
Objects that might have seemed insignificant to someone who didn’t know her, brought together into something that represents an entire life.
I think it’s extraordinary that the place where my grandmother now rests is surrounded by the small things that brought her joy.
Not her scientific papers or professional awards.
But the things she loved to collect, create, and observe.
My aunt’s work offers a different response to impermanence than the one I inherited through endurance sports.
My grandfather and mother spent years testing the limits of the body, asking how far they could go and how much they could endure.
Jessica seems to ask a different question.
What can we preserve from something that is already disappearing?
And what beauty can exist within the process of change itself?
I find it fascinating that the same extended family has approached questions of human consciousness and identity through such different disciplines.
Neuroscience.
Athletics.
Theater.
Music.
Visual art.
And now, in my own way, photography and filmmaking.
They might appear to be entirely separate pursuits, but I think they share something fundamental.
An attempt to understand what it means to be human.
What makes us who we are.
What we are capable of.
What happens when our circumstances change.
And what remains of us when the things we once believed defined our identities begin to disappear.
I sometimes wonder whether I was always destined to be drawn toward those questions.
Not because I believe our lives are predetermined, but because so much of what we become is shaped by the environments in which we grow up.
I inherited a family history filled with extraordinary achievement, but I also inherited the knowledge that achievement cannot protect us from loss.
I grew up around people who believed deeply in the value of discipline and hard work, but I have watched circumstances unfold in which neither could provide the answers we desperately wanted.
I learned to admire physical strength, but I’ve also begun to understand forms of strength that have nothing to do with athletic ability.
And perhaps most importantly, I’ve started to question the idea that a person’s identity should ever be reduced to what they can accomplish.
My grandfather is not simply the neuroscientist he was or the athlete he can no longer be.
My grandmother was never merely the illness that eventually altered her life.
My mother is not defined by the things she has been unable to change.
My aunt’s art is not valuable only because it preserves objects that might otherwise disappear.
And I don’t want to define myself exclusively through the things I create, achieve, or become.
I think we are all something more complicated than the sum of our accomplishments.
We are the relationships we form, the curiosity we sustain, the ways we respond to uncertainty, and the influence we have on people whose lives intersect with our own.
We are also vulnerable.
Painfully, unavoidably vulnerable.
And I think there is a strange kind of beauty in acknowledging that.
Because perhaps the value of a life has never depended on how completely we can control it.
Perhaps it has more to do with how deeply we participate in it while we can.
These days, when I’m back East, I try to spend at least one day a week with my grandfather at his home in White Plains.
I cook him dinner, and we talk.
In some ways, I’ve learned more about his life through those conversations than I understood during all the summers I spent with him growing up.

As a child, I knew him through experiences. Through the house in Woods Hole, the koi pond, the woodshop, and the fishing lines we improvised from old paint stirrers. I knew him as someone who seemed to have traveled everywhere and understood almost everything about the natural world.
Now, I hear more of the stories behind those experiences. About science, travel, the places he and my grandmother lived, and the remarkable collection of people they encountered through their work.
There is something strange about realizing that you can know someone your entire life and still have so much left to learn about them.
I wish the circumstances of these conversations were different.
I wish he still had the independence he once did, and that the physical world had not become so difficult for him to navigate.
But I also recognize that the time we spend together now has a significance I might not have understood when I was younger.
For so much of my childhood, he was the person introducing me to the world.
Now, sitting together over dinner, he is still doing exactly that.
Only the way we travel through it has changed.
My grandmother’s urn sits in his home.
One day, my grandfather told me that every morning he takes a small collection of pennies and rearranges them into a new design on top of the box.
He does it so that Chief can have something beautiful and different to look at each day.
And now, whenever I visit, I rearrange the pennies too.
I think about that sometimes.
My grandfather spent decades studying the mechanisms of movement, traveling the world, and testing the limits of his own physical endurance.
He accomplished things that most people will never attempt.
And now, one of the ways he expresses his love is through a small arrangement of pennies.
There is no audience for it.
No achievement to be measured.
No expectation that anyone else will ever see it.
Just a quiet act of devotion, repeated every day.
I think there is something extraordinary about that.
And perhaps it has taught me as much about the meaning of a life as any of the remarkable things he accomplished before his accident.
I think about my grandfather growing up on a farm in Iowa, with no way of knowing where his curiosity would eventually take him.
I think about my grandmother building a career around the mysteries of the brain, unaware of how personally those mysteries would one day affect her.

I think about my mother crossing the finish line in Hawaii, with my brother and me beside her, all of us too young or too caught up in the moment to understand what those memories might someday represent.
I think about my parents traveling through the Himalayas with the people who raised my mother, and the extraordinary freedom of sharing an adventure with people you love.
I think about my grandmother identifying birds outside the window, about the sewing machine and the playing cards, about shells collected from the beaches of Cape Cod.
I think about my aunt transforming fragments of those memories into art.
And I think about how little of what makes those moments meaningful can be measured.
Not in publications.
Not in finishing times.
Not in professional recognition.
Not even in the number of years someone lives.

I still admire ambition. I still believe in discipline, curiosity, and the pursuit of difficult things. I want to create meaningful work, explore the world, challenge myself, and discover what I’m capable of.
But I don’t think I want to spend my life treating achievement as proof that it has been worthwhile.
Because I have seen how quickly the circumstances that make achievement possible can change.
And I’ve begun to understand that the things we value most may not be the things we can hold onto.
A body that allows us to move freely.
A mind that allows us to recognize the people we love.
A family gathered together in a particular moment in time.
A familiar voice.
An ordinary afternoon.
The ability to wake up and choose where to go.
Perhaps the most extraordinary thing about being alive is not how much we can accomplish, but how much we are able to experience without fully recognizing the privilege of it.
And perhaps growing older is partly the process of learning to recognize that privilege before it disappears.
I don’t know whether there’s a way to reconcile the extraordinary capabilities of the human mind with the fragility of the body that contains it.
I don’t know whether loss ever becomes something we truly understand, or whether we simply learn to carry it differently.
But I do know that my family’s history has changed the way I think about freedom, success, and the meaning of a life well lived.
It has made me want to remain curious.
To take care of the people I love.
To create things that preserve something worth remembering.
To pursue experiences that make me feel fully present.
And to recognize that the ability to do any of those things is never something I should take for granted.
I think the people who came before me have spent their lives teaching me what human beings are capable of.
And through circumstances none of us would have chosen, they’ve also taught me how fragile those capabilities can be.
Perhaps the lesson is not to fear that fragility.
But to allow it to deepen our appreciation for everything that remains.
Because extraordinary things do not become less meaningful simply because they cannot last forever.
Sometimes, their impermanence is precisely what makes them extraordinary.
